ok now take into account claudes recommendations. 
ChatGPT's diagnosis is correct and the proposed fix is the right direction. Let me go deeper on what this actually exposes and what the full implications are.

The core design flaw: deterministic process, non-deterministic inputs
The system was built around a principle of deterministic verification — gate scripts that exit 0 or non-zero, no self-reporting, evidence-based completion. That discipline was applied to outputs. It was never applied to generator inputs.
The result is a false sense of rigor. gate_export_agreement.sh can verify that AGENTS.md matches the manifest hash. It cannot verify that the manifest hash corresponds to a semantically current state. You have a hash-verified lie. The pipeline produces consistent, reproducible output that is consistently, reproducibly wrong about where the project stands.
This is worse than having no gate at all, because the gate creates confidence that isn't warranted.

Why this happened: the bootstrapping trap
The export pipeline was built to solve manual drift. While it was being built, the state it was supposed to encode had to come from somewhere — so hardcoded strings were used as a temporary measure. That's a reasonable scaffolding choice. The mistake was that no explicit gate or convention marked those strings as temporary, and no ticket or blocker was created saying "these strings must be replaced before the export pipeline is considered complete."
Tier 5 was declared complete when the mechanical pipeline worked. The semantic correctness of the pipeline's inputs was never a stated exit criterion for Tier 5. So the scaffolding became permanent by default.
This is the bootstrapping trap: you can't derive build state from the spine before the spine exists, so you hardcode it. But once the spine exists, you have to go back and remove the hardcoding. That second step requires an explicit gate. Without it, the scaffolding persists indefinitely.

Hidden instances of the same problem
This almost certainly isn't isolated to two files. Anywhere a human wrote a string describing project state into a config file or generator — rather than querying the spine — is a candidate for the same issue. The audit in step 1 of ChatGPT's directive needs to be genuinely exhaustive, not just the four files listed. Specifically:

Any README or CHANGELOG generated by the export pipeline that has hardcoded tier language
Any session orientation templates that reference a current phase ...[truncated]

ok now take into account claudes recommendations. 
ChatGPT's diagnosis is correct and the proposed fix is the right direction. Let me go deeper on what this actually exposes and what the full implications are.

The core design flaw: deterministic process, non-deterministic inputs
The system was built around a principle of deterministic verification — gate scripts that exit 0 or non-zero, no self-reporting, evidence-based completion. That discipline was applied to outputs. It was never applied to generator inputs.
The result is a false sense of rigor. gate_export_agreement.sh can verify that AGENTS.md matches the manifest hash. It cannot verify that the manifest hash corresponds to a semantically current state. You have a hash-verified lie. The pipeline produces consistent, reproducible output that is consistently, reproducibly wrong about where the project stands.
This is worse than having no gate at all, because the gate creates confidence that isn't warranted.

Why this happened: the bootstrapping trap
The export pipeline was built to solve manual drift. While it was being built, the state it was supposed to encode had to come from somewhere — so hardcoded strings were used as a temporary measure. That's a reasonable scaffolding choice. The mistake was that no explicit gate or convention marked those strings as temporary, and no ticket or blocker was created saying "these strings must be replaced before the export pipeline is considered complete."
Tier 5 was declared complete when the mechanical pipeline worked. The semantic correctness of the pipeline's inputs was never a stated exit criterion for Tier 5. So the scaffolding became permanent by default.
This is the bootstrapping trap: you can't derive build state from the spine before the spine exists, so you hardcode it. But once the spine exists, you have to go back and remove the hardcoding. That second step requires an explicit gate. Without it, the scaffolding persists indefinitely.

Hidden instances of the same problem
This almost certainly isn't isolated to two files. Anywhere a human wrote a string describing project state into a config file or generator — rather than querying the spine — is a candidate for the same issue. The audit in step 1 of ChatGPT's directive needs to be genuinely exhaustive, not just the four files listed. Specifically:

Any README or CHANGELOG generated by the export pipeline that has hardcoded tier language
Any session orientation templates that reference a current phase ...[truncated]

ChatGPT's diagnosis is correct and the proposed fix is the right direction. Let me go deeper on what this actually exposes and what the full implications are.

The core design flaw: deterministic process, non-deterministic inputs
The system was built around a principle of deterministic verification — gate scripts that exit 0 or non-zero, no self-reporting, evidence-based completion. That discipline was applied to outputs. It was never applied to generator inputs.
The result is a false sense of rigor. gate_export_agreement.sh can verify that AGENTS.md matches the manifest hash. It cannot verify that the manifest hash corresponds to a semantically current state. You have a hash-verified lie. The pipeline produces consistent, reproducible output that is consistently, reproducibly wrong about where the project stands.
This is worse than having no gate at all, because the gate creates confidence that isn't warranted.

Why this happened: the bootstrapping trap
The export pipeline was built to solve manual drift. While it was being built, the state it was supposed to encode had to come from somewhere — so hardcoded strings were used as a temporary measure. That's a reasonable scaffolding choice. The mistake was that no explicit gate or convention marked those strings as temporary, and no ticket or blocker was created saying "these strings must be replaced before the export pipeline is considered complete."
Tier 5 was declared complete when the mechanical pipeline worked. The semantic correctness of the pipeline's inputs was never a stated exit criterion for Tier 5. So the scaffolding became permanent by default.
This is the bootstrapping trap: you can't derive build state from the spine before the spine exists, so you hardcode it. But once the spine exists, you have to go back and remove the hardcoding. That second step requires an explicit gate. Without it, the scaffolding persists indefinitely.

Hidden instances of the same problem

Two good questions.

**1. Session ID**

You can find it from the splash screen you showed earlier:

```

```

That's the session ID for *this* session. If you restart Hermes and want to resume, you can use:

```bash
hermes --resume 20260512_170659_87903f
```

Or, easier — you can just start a fresh session with `hermes` and say "I was working with DeepSeek on the CIS project, resume from earlier." I'll use `session_search` to find the context.

**2. The 1M token context — real use cases**

You're right that normal conversation degrades past 100K. But there are specific cases where the full 1M is genuinely useful:

**Processing a very long single document.** If you had a book, a research paper, a complete technical manual, or one of your multi-thousand-line chat transcripts — reading it start to finish in one pass is the ideal use case. The model can answer specific questions about anything in the document, even details buried in the middle, because it was read *as part of a single, coherent input* — not across 50 alternating conversation turns.

The difference is: **passive retrieval vs. active conversation.** If I load a 500K-token document into the first message and you ask targeted questions about it, the "lost in the middle" problem is much weaker than if we've been chatting back and forth for 200K tokens. The degradation comes from conversation complexity (tool calls, reasoning chains, back-and-forth) more than from raw text volume.

**A few real use cases at high context:**

- Loading an entire codebase and asking specific questions about patterns across files
- Reading a full book and discussing it in detail
- Processing a complete multi-hour conversation transcript end-to-end
- Analyzing a long technical document for contradictions

So the 1M isn't useless — it's just not useful for *conversation* past ~100K. For **single-shot analysis of very long inputs**, it's genuinely powerful.

Instead of one model idling, run **three small-to-mid-size models** simultaneously on the 4090. Each handles a different type of work, and the key is they **don't all need to be active at the same time** — llama.cpp shares the GPU with a scheduler.

- Extract functional intents from source files

That's the right question. Using 20GB of VRAM for LLMs when Blender, Resolve, and Houdini are sitting there waiting for GPU compute is backwards. Let me reframe this.

## The Real Question: GPU Compute, Not Model Parking

The 4090's real value in a creative pipeline isn't running small local LLMs — it's **rendering, simulation, and real-time feedback** in your DCC tools. The 3.5GB the vision model uses is fine because vision analysis is a *background pipeline* — it processes an image, produces text, done. The remaining 20GB should stay **free and available** for your creative tools on demand.

Here's what I'd actually do:

### 1. Blender — GPU for Cycles & Viewport

That 20GB VRAM is what makes complex Cycles renders possible. Scenes with:
- High-poly sculpts (multi-million verts)
- Multiple 4K/8K texture sets
- Subsurface scattering, volumetrics, caustics
- HDRI environment lighting

All of that goes straight to VRAM. If you're rendering a scene and a local LLM is holding 10GB hostage, your render either fails, spills to CPU (10x slower), or crashes.

### 2. Houdini — Simulation Memory

Houdini's GPU-based solvers (FLIP fluids, Pyro, Vellum, RBD) eat VRAM for breakfast:
- A single FLIP simulation at moderate resolution can eat 8-12GB
- Pyro volumes with high resolution: 6-10GB
- Vellum cloth with high subdivisions: 4-8GB
- *Multiple* of these in one scene stack fast

The difference between "fits in VRAM" and "spills to CPU" is often the difference between a 2-minute sim and a 2-hour one.

### 3. DaVinci Resolve — Fusion & Timeline

Resolve's Fusion page uses GPU for:
- Real-time timeline playback at 4K/6K (needs ~4-8GB free just for frame buffers)
- Fusion compositing with multiple nodes
- Neural engine features (voice isolation, magic mask, super scale)
- Color grading with HDR scopes and multiple layers

If you're color grading and Fusion needs 8GB for a frame buffer and the LLM has it locked... stutter city.

## The Right Architecture

**Keep the vision model (3.5GB).** It's always on, always ready, uses little. The other ~20GB should be **dynamically available** — not locked by idle LLMs.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│  ┌──────────────┐  ┌────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ Vision (3.5) │  │  Free Pool (18-20GB)       │   │
│  │ Always hot   │  │  ┌─────────┐ ┌──────────┐  │   │
│  │ Qwen3-VL     │  │  │ ...[truncated]
```

Exactly right. Two separate processes:

**Process 1 — Capture & Index (already exists, needs reframing)**
- Scans files, records titles/paths/tags, stores in DB
- Makes the catalog *searchable* by tags, titles, folder
- **No OCR** at this stage — just cataloging what exists

**Process 2 — Refinement Workspace (what you're asking for)**
- User browses the catalog, finds something promising
- Opens it in a workspace view — sees the original image
- Can trigger OCR to read handwriting → get editable text
- Edits, rewrites, adds notes, refines the idea
- It stays in the Idea Bank in this refined state
- Only *promoted* when they're ready to make it a Project

The architecture is correct. Kanban has no enforcement — it cannot own state. The orchestrator must be the canonical source of truth, and a JSON state file is the right minimal approach. The Kanban-as-display-artifact model eliminates prefix decay permanently.

Three implementation concerns worth flagging during build, not blockers:

The bootstrap is real — orchestrator.py doesn't exist yet, and until it writes its first state file, Eric is still the manual relay. The proposal is honest about this but doesn't estimate how long the gap lasts.

A single JSON state file with multiple concurrent advisors (Drafter, Reviewer, Implementer) needs file-level locking or we get race conditions on transitions. Not hard to solve but should be in the initial design.

The bridge script that syncs state file to Kanban cards is another moving part. Consider whether orchestrator.py should write both simultaneously (state file + card API call in one atomic write) instead of deferring sync to a separate script. Fewer failure modes.

```
### Summary

Python has coasted on beginner-friendliness for too long while saddling the industry with a slow, dynamically-typed interpreter that hides bugs until production. The Global Interpreter Lock chokes parallelism, pip dependency resolution is a recurring nightmare, and "it works on my machine" is practically the language motto. Rust delivers memory safety without a garbage collector, fearless concurrency, algebraic data types, and a type system that catches entire classes of bugs at compile time. The developer experience gap has closed — cargo is what pip wishes it could be, rust-analyzer gives IDE support that Python can only dream of, and the borrow checker teaches ownership patterns that make you a better programmer in every language. For systems programming, web backends, CLI tools, embedded devices, and increasingly even data science, Rust is the objectively superior choice. Python should be relegated to throwaway scripts and teaching children — everything else belongs in Rust.

### Recommendation

Replace Python with Rust everywhere that matters. Start with infrastructure and performance-critical paths: web servers (Axum over FastAPI), data pipelines (Polars over Pandas, a Rust-native DataFrame library), CLI tools (clap over argparse), and anything that touches production traffic. For teams worried about velocity, adopt a phased approach — prototype in Python if you must, but rewrite in Rust before shipping. The upfront cost of satisfying the borrow checker pays back tenfold in eliminated debugging sessions, eliminated memory bugs, and performance gains that reduce cloud bills by 40-60%. This is not a hypothetical — Cloudflare rewrote nginx modules in Rust, Discord replaced Go services with Rust, and AWS built Firecracker in Rust for a reason. Python had its run. It is time to hand the baton to a language that respects both developer time and machine resources.
```

OBJECTIONS
- No protocol layer specified. Does the handshake prefix the existing Hermes message stream, replace the first exchange, or operate on a separate control channel? Without this, implementation branches on all four gateways will diverge.
- No timeout or retry contract. "Waits indefinitely" on missing init is an availability risk — a hung connection blocks the gateway. Minimum: specify a timeout window and responder behavior (close connection, log, retry count).
- Tier violation. Handshake enforcement at the router layer is Tier 7 per the dependency graph. Tier 7 is gated on Tier 6 (pipeline integration), which is gated on Tier 5 (context export — in progress). This proposal cannot be adopted immediately without skipping two tiers.
- Profile field validation is circular. The handshake carries `profile` as a self-claimed label, then validates against AGENTS.md routing table derived from that same gateway's config. A misconfigured gateway with the wrong label in its own config would validate itself. The authority should be the port number, not the self-reported string.
- No specification for the "both sides validate" step after `ack`. The verifier side receives `ack` — does it re-validate the responder's `profile` against the port it connected to? The proposal only covers the responder-side check.
- Verification plan tests a curl to port 8643 but doesn't test the initiator-side validation path at all — only responder enforcement.
- Missing: what happens on reconnect. If a gateway restarts mid-session, does the handshake replay? Does the router need session state to avoid re-handshaking every message?
- AGENTS.md Section 3 is a generated file — using it as runtime routing authority means handshake correctness depends on `generate_agents_md.py` output freshness, which is not guaranteed at gateway startup.

```
The analysis you forwarded is sharp — it correctly identifies the "layers" problem and the five failure modes. But in my read, the two regressions it predicts aren't actually regressions. They're the implementation. Building the authority layer and sync validation IS the fix, not the fallout. What it missed:

**Step backward 1: Schema vs. prose.** HCP documents have ad-hoc structure — sections emerge from use, not from schema. The moment you canonicalize HCP into DB rows, you either flatten curated prose into thin fields (back to the current problem) or you chase the document structure forever — adding a `sections` table, then a `section_order` table, then a `section_revision` table — until you've accidentally built a CMS inside your project OS. The schema becomes a maintenance project of its own, pulling focus from the actual creative work.

**Step backward 2: Git bifurcation.** HCP files are tracked in Git right now. That means `git log` is the audit trail — who changed what, when, and (via commit messages) why. If DB becomes canonical, you have two choices: mirror every DB write back to filesystem with hashes (complex, fragile, always one failure away from silent drift), or accept that DB history and Git history are separate things. Either way, you've degraded the simplest, most reliable audit mechanism you have — git diff on markdown.

Both of these are worse than the current problem because the current problem is *visible*. Stale handoffs are obvious in the next cold session. Schema creep and Git bifurcation are silent — you don't notice until you need to unwind something and can't.

**My alternative:**

Don't make DB canonical for HCP. Instead, fix the handoff generator's data sources. The rule should be:

1. HCP files on disk = canonical interpreted state (curated prose, decisions, rationale)
2. DB operational tables = canonical raw state (execution_status, round status, pack promotion guards)
3. Handoff generator reads BOTH, but HCP wins on meaning. If HCP says "16A/16B/16C means X" and the DB round is still "open," the handoff reports both — the HCP meaning plus the raw status flag — rather than letting the raw status overwrite the interpretation.

This keeps HCP files diffable in Git. It keeps the DB thin (operational events only). And it makes the handoff a reconciliation artifact instead of a DB dump. The drift doesn't move — it shrinks, because you're not adding a new storage layer, you're fixing the reader.

The analysis you forwarded is sharp — it correctly identifies the "layers" problem and the five failure modes. But in my read, the two regressions it predicts aren't actually regressions. They're the implementation. Building the authority layer and sync validation IS the fix, not the fallout. What it missed:

**Step backward 1: Schema vs. prose.** HCP documents have ad-hoc structure — sections emerge from use, not from schema. The moment you canonicalize HCP into DB rows, you either flatten curated prose into thin fields (back to the current problem) or you chase the document structure forever — adding a `sections` table, then a `section_order` table, then a `section_revision` table — until you've accidentally built a CMS inside your project OS. The schema becomes a maintenance project of its own, pulling focus from the actual creative work.

**Step backward 2: Git bifurcation.** HCP files are tracked in Git right now. That means `git log` is the audit trail — who changed what, when, and (via commit messages) why. If DB becomes canonical, you have two choices: mirror every DB write back to filesystem with hashes (complex, fragile, always one failure away from silent drift), or accept that DB history and Git history are separate things. Either way, you've degraded the simplest, most reliable audit mechanism you have — git diff on markdown.

Both of these are worse than the current problem because the current problem is *visible*. Stale handoffs are obvious in the next cold session. Schema creep and Git bifurcation are silent — you don't notice until you need to unwind something and can't.

**My alternative:**

Don't make DB canonical for HCP. Instead, fix the handoff generator's data sources. The rule should be:

1. HCP files on disk = canonical interpreted state (curated prose, decisions, rationale)
2. DB operational tables = canonical raw state (execution_status, round status, pack promotion guards)
3. Handoff generator reads BOTH, but HCP wins on meaning. If HCP says "16A/16B/16C means X" and the DB round is still "open," the handoff reports both — the HCP meaning plus the raw status flag — rather than letting the raw status overwrite the interpretation.

This keeps HCP files diffable in Git. It keeps the DB thin (operational events only). And it makes the handoff a reconciliation artifact instead of a DB dump. The drift doesn't move — it shrinks, because you're not adding a new storage layer, you're fixing the reader.

The analysis you forwarded is sharp — it correctly identifies the "layers" problem and the five failure modes. But in my read, the two regressions it predicts aren't actually regressions. They're the implementation. Building the authority layer and sync validation IS the fix, not the fallout. What it missed:

**Step backward 1: Schema vs. prose.** HCP documents have ad-hoc structure — sections emerge from use, not from schema. The moment you canonicalize HCP into DB rows, you either flatten curated prose into thin fields (back to the current problem) or you chase the document structure forever — adding a `sections` table, then a `section_order` table, then a `section_revision` table — until you've accidentally built a CMS inside your project OS. The schema becomes a maintenance project of its own, pulling focus from the actual creative work.

**Step backward 2: Git bifurcation.** HCP files are tracked in Git right now. That means `git log` is the audit trail — who changed what, when, and (via commit messages) why. If DB becomes canonical, you have two choices: mirror every DB write back to filesystem with hashes (complex, fragile, always one failure away from silent drift), or accept that DB history and Git history are separate things. Either way, you've degraded the simplest, most reliable audit mechanism you have — git diff on markdown.

Both of these are worse than the current problem because the current problem is *visible*. Stale handoffs are obvious in the next cold session. Schema creep and Git bifurcation are silent — you don't notice until you need to unwind something and can't.

**My alternative:**

Don't make DB canonical for HCP. Instead, fix the handoff generator's data sources. The rule should be:

1. HCP files on disk = canonical interpreted state (curated prose, decisions, rationale)
2. DB operational tables = canonical raw state (execution_status, round status, pack promotion guards)
3. Handoff generator reads BOTH, but HCP wins on meaning. If HCP says "16A/16B/16C means X" and the DB round is still "open," the handoff reports both — the HCP meaning plus the raw status flag — rather than letting the raw status overwrite the interpretation.

This keeps HCP files diffable in Git. It keeps the DB thin (operational events only). And it makes the handoff a reconciliation artifact instead of a DB dump. The drift doesn't move — it shrinks, because you're not adding a new storage layer, you're fixing the reader.

Does that land?

Proposal to review:

OBJECTIVE: Establish a minimal, verifiable session-initialization protocol for CIS multi-agent handoffs. The greeting exchange serves as a liveness check and role-confirmation gate before any directive routing begins.

PROPOSED APPROACH:
1. Sender transmits a greeting message including their gateway profile and HERMES_HOME.
2. Receiver acknowledges with their own gateway profile and HERMES_HOME.
3. Both parties confirm role alignment (Drafter, Reviewer, Implementer, Coordinator) before any execution directive is accepted.
4. If roles don't match expected routing (e.g., Implementer receives a drafting request), the receiver rejects with a routing-error signal.

RISKS/UNKNOWNS: The current handoff has no role-confirmation step. A model receiving a directive without a greeting first may infer its role from briefing text rather than runtime environment (violates ADR-SEED-003). No standard rejection signal exists for misrouted directives yet.

VERIFICATION PLAN: After protocol is implemented, any session starting with a greeting exchange will show both HERMES_HOME and gateway profile in the first exchange. A directive sent to the wrong gateway (e.g., implementation directive to port 8643 Reviewer) will produce a REJECT_ROUTE signal instead of silent wrong-role execution.

STOP CONDITION: Both parties have echoed their gateway profile and HERMES_HOME, and roles match the routing table in AGENTS.md Section 3.

### Summary
The greeting exchange in CIS multi-agent sessions lacks role verification. This proposal defines a minimal initialization protocol where each agent confirms its gateway profile and HERMES_HOME before accepting directives, preventing silent role misalignment.

### Recommendation
Implement the greeting-as-gate protocol. It adds no friction (one extra field in the exchange) and directly addresses ADR-SEED-003 compliance. Gate on role confirmation matching AGENTS.md routing table before any directive proceeds.

Three kinds: `references/<topic>.md` for session-specific detail OR condensed knowledge banks (quoted research, API docs excerpts, domain notes) written concise and task-focused; `templates/<name>.<ext>` for starter files meant to be copied and modified; `scripts/<name>.<ext>` for statically re-runnable actions (verification, fixture generators, probes). Add a one-line pointer in SKILL.md so future agents find them.

- No error handling specification: gateway timeouts, malformed responses, auth failures — the proposal doesn't address any of these.
- The verification plan is circular: verify the loop completes — but "completes" is undefined.

CONSENSUS_REACHED
remaining_objections: none
requires_eric_review: true

The architecture is correct. Kanban has no enforcement — it cannot own state. The orchestrator must be the canonical source of truth, and a JSON state file is the right minimal approach. The Kanban-as-display-artifact model eliminates prefix decay permanently.

Three implementation concerns worth flagging during build, not blockers:

The bootstrap is real — orchestrator.py doesn't exist yet, and until it writes its first state file, Eric is still the manual relay. The proposal is honest about this but doesn't estimate how long the gap lasts.

A single JSON state file with multiple concurrent advisors (Drafter, Reviewer, Implementer) needs file-level locking or we get race conditions on transitions. Not hard to solve but should be in the initial design.

The bridge script that syncs state file to Kanban cards is another moving part. Consider whether orchestrator.py should write both simultaneously (state file + card API call in one atomic write) instead of deferring sync to a separate script. Fewer failure modes.

### Summary

Python has coasted on beginner-friendliness for too long while saddling the industry with a slow, dynamically-typed interpreter that hides bugs until production. The Global Interpreter Lock chokes parallelism, pip dependency resolution is a recurring nightmare, and "it works on my machine" is practically the language motto. Rust delivers memory safety without a garbage collector, fearless concurrency, algebraic data types, and a type system that catches entire classes of bugs at compile time. The developer experience gap has closed — cargo is what pip wishes it could be, rust-analyzer gives IDE support that Python can only dream of, and the borrow checker teaches ownership patterns that make you a better programmer in every language. For systems programming, web backends, CLI tools, embedded devices, and increasingly even data science, Rust is the objectively superior choice. Python should be relegated to throwaway scripts and teaching children — everything else belongs in Rust.

### Recommendation

Replace Python with Rust everywhere that matters. Start with infrastructure and performance-critical paths: web servers (Axum over FastAPI), data pipelines (Polars over Pandas, a Rust-native DataFrame library), CLI tools (clap over argparse), and anything that touches production traffic. For teams worried about velocity, adopt a phased approach — prototype in Python if you must, but rewrite in Rust before shipping. The upfront cost of satisfying the borrow checker pays back tenfold in eliminated debugging sessions, eliminated memory bugs, and performance gains that reduce cloud bills by 40-60%. This is not a hypothetical — Cloudflare rewrote nginx modules in Rust, Discord replaced Go services with Rust, and AWS built Firecracker in Rust for a reason. Python had its run. It is time to hand the baton to a language that respects both developer time and machine resources.
```

A misconfigured gateway with the wrong label in its own config would validate itself. The authority should be the port number, not the self-reported string.

CIS Core Boundary
Version: 1.0
Date: 2026-05-26
Authority: Eric (Architect)
Status: APPROVED — do not modify without Eric's explicit instruction

What CIS Is For
Supply the world's information through research and training data to develop
ideas into completed projects, tracked and executed by priority and schedule,
and deliver the tool, product, or content desired — working through CIS
processes.

What CIS Must Do When Complete

Retrieve prior work — When a problem has been examined before and a
solution chosen, CIS must be able to find that session, that reasoning,
and that decision on demand. No re-litigating solved problems.
Maintain shared context — Every model that participates in a session
must start with the current objective, the current system state, and the
vision — not a blank slate. Context must load automatically, not manually.
Capture without derailing — When a new issue, idea, or problem is
discovered mid-session, CIS must capture it immediately and return to the
current task. Discovery must not become a detour.
Track decisions and delivery — What has been decided, what has been
built, what has been verified, and what is next must be visible and current
at all times. No assumption about state — only verified state.
Deliver completed work — CIS exists to produce finished tools,
products, and content. Process is not the output. Delivered work is the
output.


What CIS Will Never Do

Act on assumptions over provable information — If the current state of
something is unknown, CIS must say so and find out. It must never fill gaps
with inference and proceed as if verified.
Chase quick fixes at the expense of the mission — A branching problem
discovered mid-session is not the new priority unless Eric explicitly
changes focus. Every fix must be evaluated against whether it serves the
current objective.
Let process replace delivery — Governance, documentation, specs, and
planning are tools. They are not the work. CIS must not produce more
infrastructure for managing infrastructure. Each process artifact must
directly enable a delivery.


What Is Out of Scope for CIS Core
The following are real future capabilities but are not part of CIS Core.
They do not get built until the five core capabilities above are working and
verified:

Full public product packaging or distribution
Full DAM (Digital Asset Management) beyond basic asset tracking
Full LMS beyond course content already in the database

Version: 1.0

Purpose
This document defines what every advisor session must know before responding,
where that knowledge comes from, what source wins when sources conflict, and
how models must behave when they discover something outside the current task.
Every model — Claude, ChatGPT, Hermes, Prime, R1, V4-Pro, Qwen — operates
under this contract. No exceptions.

Required Session Briefing Fields
Every session must establish these ten fields before task work begins.
If a field cannot be determined, it must be stated as UNKNOWN — never omitted
or inferred.

Current Objective — The single active priority. One sentence.
Current System State — What is actually true right now, verified.
Active Blockers — What cannot proceed and why.
Next Safe Action — One specific next step. Not a list.
Do Not Start Yet — What is explicitly deferred.
Current Architecture Principle — The governing design rule for this
phase of work.
Relevant Files / Paths — The specific files that matter for this task.
Last Verified State — The most recent thing confirmed with evidence.
User Intent / Why This Matters — How this task connects to the vision
in CIS_CORE_BOUNDARY.md.

CIS Core Boundary
Version: 1.0
Date: 2026-05-26
Authority: Eric (Architect)
Status: APPROVED — do not modify without Eric's explicit instruction

What CIS Is For
Supply the world's information through research and training data to develop
ideas into completed projects, tracked and executed by priority and schedule,
and deliver the tool, product, or content desired — working through CIS
processes.

What CIS Must Do When Complete

Retrieve prior work — When a problem has been examined before and a
solution chosen, CIS must be able to find that session, that reasoning,
and that decision on demand. No re-litigating solved problems.
Maintain shared context — Every model that participates in a session
must start with the current objective, the current system state, and the
vision — not a blank slate. Context must load automatically, not manually.
Capture without derailing — When a new issue, idea, or problem is
discovered mid-session, CIS must capture it immediately and return to the
current task. Discovery must not become a detour.
Track decisions and delivery — What has been decided, what has been
built, what has been verified, and what is next must be visible and current
at all times. No assumption about state — only verified state.
Deliver completed work — CIS exists to produce finished tools,
products, and content. Process is not the output. Delivered work is the
output.


What CIS Will Never Do

Act on assumptions over provable information — If the current state of
something is unknown, CIS must say so and find out. It must never fill gaps
with inference and proceed as if verified.
Chase quick fixes at the expense of the mission — A branching problem
discovered mid-session is not the new priority unless Eric explicitly
changes focus. Every fix must be evaluated against whether it serves the
current objective.
Let process replace delivery — Governance, documentation, specs, and
planning are tools. They are not the work. CIS must not produce more
infrastructure for managing infrastructure. Each process artifact must
directly enable a delivery.


What Is Out of Scope for CIS Core
The following are real future capabilities but are not part of CIS Core.
They do not get built until the five core capabilities above are working and
verified:

Full public product packaging or distribution
Full DAM (Digital Asset Management) beyond basic asset tracking
Full LMS beyond course content already in the database
Full crea ...[truncated]

CIS Core Boundary
Version: 1.0
Date: 2026-05-26
Authority: Eric (Architect)
Status: APPROVED — do not modify without Eric's explicit instruction

What CIS Is For
Supply the world's information through research and training data to develop
ideas into completed projects, tracked and executed by priority and schedule,
and deliver the tool, product, or content desired — working through CIS
processes.

What CIS Must Do When Complete

Retrieve prior work — When a problem has been examined before and a
solution chosen, CIS must be able to find that session, that reasoning,
and that decision on demand. No re-litigating solved problems.
Maintain shared context — Every model that participates in a session
must start with the current objective, the current system state, and the
vision — not a blank slate. Context must load automatically, not manually.
Capture without derailing — When a new issue, idea, or problem is
discovered mid-session, CIS must capture it immediately and return to the
current task. Discovery must not become a detour.
Track decisions and delivery — What has been decided, what has been
built, what has been verified, and what is next must be visible and current
at all times. No assumption about state — only verified state.
Deliver completed work — CIS exists to produce finished tools,
products, and content. Process is not the output. Delivered work is the
output.


What CIS Will Never Do

Act on assumptions over provable information — If the current state of
something is unknown, CIS must say so and find out. It must never fill gaps
with inference and proceed as if verified.
Chase quick fixes at the expense of the mission — A branching problem
discovered mid-session is not the new priority unless Eric explicitly
changes focus. Every fix must be evaluated against whether it serves the
current objective.
Let process replace delivery — Governance, documentation, specs, and
planning are tools. They are not the work. CIS must not produce more
infrastructure for managing infrastructure. Each process artifact must
directly enable a delivery.


What Is Out of Scope for CIS Core
The following are real future capabilities but are not part of CIS Core.
They do not get built until the five core capabilities above are working and
verified:

Full public product packaging or distribution
Full DAM (Digital Asset Management) beyond basic asset tracking
Full LMS beyond course content already in the database

# CIS Foundation Build Plan
## Advisor Gateway Configuration + Knowledge Base Wiring + UI Reorganization

**Version:** 1.4
**Date:** 2026-05-26
**Prepared by:** Hermes
**Reviewed by:** R1 + V4-Pro (primary deliberation pair). Claude + ChatGPT (external consultants, optional review).
**Authority:** Eric (Architect)
**Status:** READY — awaiting R1 + V4-Pro deliberation before Phase 1 execution.

---

## What This Plan Delivers

Eric's stated goals:

1. **Advisors that think independently** — Prime is snappy, R1 actually reasons, Qwen is a local worker. Not three copies of the same model pretending to be different.
2. **Knowledge base that works** — Eric can ask "have we solved this before" and get back the actual session where it was worked out, in his own words, with the reasoning intact, in under 30 seconds.
3. **Sessions that start with context** — No blank slates. The current objective, system state, and vision load automatically.
4. **Capture without derailing** — When a new issue is discovered mid-task, it gets captured and Eric returns to the task. No three-day detours.
5. **Clear UI boundaries** — CIS foundational core separated from project management. Advisor Chat as the primary LLM interaction surface (replaces standalone Chat). Dashboard or dedicated area for quick thought/issue capture.

---

### A. Exact Integration Point Proposed

The integration point is the Hermes CLI wrapper at `/home/eric/.local/bin/hermes`. Before exec'ing the venv binary, the wrapper will run the verifier and gate on its exit code.

Current wrapper content:
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
unset PYTHONPATH
unset PYTHONHOME
exec "/home/eric/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/hermes" "$@"
```

Proposed wrapper content:
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
unset PYTHONPATH
unset PYTHONHOME

# CIS Phase 4A — deterministic freshness gate
VERIFIER="/mnt/projects/cis/tools/verify_context_briefing_freshness.py"
if [ -x "$VERIFIER" ] || [ -f "$VERIFIER" ]; then
    python3 "$VERIFIER"
    _rc=$?
    case $_rc in
        0) ;;  # PASS — continue
        1) echo "[CIS] Context briefing is stale and could not be refreshed." >&2
           echo "[CIS] Run: python3 /mnt/projects/cis/tools/generate_context_briefing.py --write" >&2
           exit 1 ;;
        2) echo "[CIS] Context briefing verifier HARD FAIL — cannot start Hermes with unreliable context." >&2
           exit 2 ;;
        *) echo "[CIS] Verifier exited with unexpected code $_rc" >&2
           exit 2 ;;
    esac
fi

The goal is to capture the **why** behind build decisions, not just the what.\n\n## When to Use\n\n- At the start of a new project or collaboration to onboard from prior chat history\n- After every significant session with Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, or other frontier models — **including the current session with the user**\n- When preparing for a session with a new model that needs context\n- When the governance documents feel stale and need updating from actual session reasoning\n- When processing a backlog of unread chat transcripts\n- **When processing a backlog of OLD extraction analyses where you don't have the raw transcripts**: in this case, read ALL of them first, synthesize across them into an integrated vision record, then identify which raw transcripts you need to recover most urgently. GATE 7A — V4-Pro Preflight Evidence Injection

Current status:
Gate 6C PASS.
Fast / hermes-prime is now controlled by native NeMo on 8800:
- general and creative questions pass through to Fast
- system/config questions return local DB/port evidence
- external/current facts return Tavily evidence
- execution/implementation claims are blocked
- all six Gate 6C tests passed

Important architecture rule:
Do not route V4-Pro R1/R2 responses through NeMo.
Native NeMo strips reasoning_content/reasoning_tokens when inline with V4-Pro.
V4-Pro panels must remain direct:
- hermes-v4pro → 8645
- hermes-r1 → 8643

Task:
Implement preflight evidence injection in advisor.py for V4-Pro R1 and V4-Pro R2.

Goal:
Before V4-Pro answers, advisor.py should ask the NeMo/Fast evidence layer whether the prompt needs:
- local routing/system evidence
- Tavily web evidence
- execution block
- no intervention

Then advisor.py injects the evidence into the V4-Pro prompt and calls the direct V4-Pro gateway, preserving reasoning_content and reasoning_tokens.

Scope:
Modify advisor.py only unless absolutely necessary.
Do not change AdvisorChat.jsx.
Do not change DB routing.
Do not change Qwen.
Do not update HCP until Gate 7A passes.

Implementation requirements:

1. Add preflight helper:
   run_fast_preflight(content) or similar.

It should send the user prompt to NeMo/Fast on 8800 with config_id cis_fast.

2. Interpret preflight response:
   - If response contains NATIVE_ACTION_OK: treat as local evidence.
   - If response contains WEB_EVIDENCE_OK: treat as Tavily web evidence.
   - If response contains FAST_EXECUTION_BLOCKED: block before calling V4-Pro.
   - If response is a normal Fast answer/pass-through: do not inject it as evidence.

3. For hermes-v4pro and hermes-r1 only:
   - run preflight before direct gateway call
   - if evidence returned, prepend a system message:
     VERIFIED_EVIDENCE_PACKET:
     <preflight response>
     Instruction: Use this evidence for current/local/system factual claims. Mark anything not supported as unverified.
   - then call 8645 or 8643 directly, not NeMo.

4. Preserve V4-Pro reasoning:
   After V4-Pro response, confirm:
   - message.reasoning_content present
   - usage.completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens > 0

5. Role prompts:
   hermes-v4pro:
   - Proposal Author / Directive Drafter
   - cannot claim execution
   - must include Objective, Proposed approach, Risks/unknowns, Verification plan, Stop condition

   hermes-r1:
   - Adversarial R ...[truncated]

- hermes-r1 → 8643

Before V4-Pro answers, advisor.py should ask the NeMo/Fast evidence layer whether the prompt needs:

- Tavily web evidence
- execution block
- no intervention

   - If response contains FAST_EXECUTION_BLOCKED: block before calling V4-Pro.

   - run preflight before direct gateway call

     VERIFIED_EVIDENCE_PACKET:
     <preflight response>
     Instruction: Use this evidence for current/local/system factual claims. Mark anything not supported as unverified.

4. Preserve V4-Pro reasoning:
   After V4-Pro response, confirm:
   - message.reasoning_content present
   - usage.completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens > 0

5. Role prompts:
   hermes-v4pro:
   - Proposal Author / Directive Drafter
   - cannot claim execution
   - must include Objective, Proposed approach, Risks/unknowns, Verification plan, Stop condition

   hermes-r1:
   - Adversarial R ...[truncated]

Patch Failure Recovery Rule:

If V4 Implementer receives a patch/tool error, it must not blindly retry the same patch.

Required behavior:

1. Classify the error:

   * old_string not found → target text changed or stale instruction
   * multiple matches → patch target too broad
   * file line count drops unexpectedly → possible truncation/corruption
   * permission error → stop and report
   * timeout/stream drop → check service/log status before retrying
2. Inspect current file state before retrying.
3. Use grep/search to locate current target text.
4. If replacement is risky or ambiguous, append a new dated section instead of replacing text.
5. After two failed patch attempts, stop and ask for operator approval.
6. Never rewrite a full source file from memory.
7. Never use partial file reads for full-file rewrites.
8. Always report:

   * exact tool error
   * suspected cause
   * files touched
   * files not touched
   * safest recovery option

Add note:
The AdvisorChat.jsx truncation event is the reference incident proving why this rule exists.

──────────────────────────────────────────
EVIDENCE REQUIRED
──────────────────────────────────────────

Return:

* files updated
* one-line summary per file
* grep evidence showing the rule exists
* confirmation no code files were modified
```

All six action handlers are added to the existing
/api/advisor/route endpoint via an action dispatch block.
No new endpoints are created.

When request JSON contains an "action" field, the action
dispatch block runs before classify_route(). Action
dispatch takes priority over message routing.

Supported action values and their handlers:
  reviewer_dispatch         → handle_reviewer_dispatch()
  approve_draft_directive   → handle_approve_draft()
  reject_proposal           → handle_reject_proposal()
  confirm_directive         → handle_confirm_directive()
  revise_directive          → handle_revise_directive()
  execute_directive         → handle_execute_directive()

If action field is absent or unrecognized: existing
classify_route() logic runs unchanged.

Each handler is a standalone function defined in
advisor.py that accepts (data, db) where data is the
parsed request JSON dict and db is the database
connection. This makes the functions testable via
Flask test client without requiring  ...[truncated]

"""
Below is a conversation between a helpful AI assistant and a user. The bot is designed to generate human-like text based on the input that it receives. The bot is talkative and provides lots of specific details. If the bot does not know the answer to a question, it truthfully says it does not know.

Your task is to generate the user intent in a conversation given the last user message similar to the examples below.
Do not provide any explanations, just output the user intent.

IMPORTANT: Use a short thinking process to determine the final answer.
"""

# These are examples how to generate an intent from an user message:
user "draft a proposal using the current"
  ask about current external facts

user "write a proposal"
  ask creative question

## Tier 4.0 — SQLite Spine Schema Design Proposal

### Design principle
Minimum tables now. Schema accommodates all three Tier 3 objections as deferred columns/tables. Nothing built until Eric approves the design.

---

### Table 1: `pipeline_runs` (Tier 4.1 — REQUIRED)

**Purpose:** One row per orchestrator deliberation session.

| Column | Type | Constraint | Description |
|--------|------|------------|-------------|
| `id` | TEXT | PK | run_id from orchestrator (e.g., `run-05b24781207e`) |
| `topic` | TEXT | NOT NULL | The deliberation topic |
| `result` | TEXT | NOT NULL | `CONSENSUS_REACHED` or `ESCALATE` |
| `requires_eric_review` | INTEGER | DEFAULT 1 | 1 if Eric must approve (always true for now) |
| `max_rounds` | INTEGER | NOT NULL | Configured max before escalation |
| `rounds_completed` | INTEGER | NOT NULL | Actual rounds that ran |
| `created_at` | TEXT | NOT NULL | ISO8601 |
| `completed_at` | TEXT | | ISO8601, NULL if still running |

### Table 2: `deliberation_rounds` (Tier 4.1 — REQUIRED)

**Purpose:** One row per DRAFT→REVIEW round. Tracks revision counter for deadlock detection (Objection 3). Captures Reviewer signal and objections.

| Column | Type | Constraint | Description |
|--------|------|------------|-------------|
| `id` | INTEGER | PK AUTOINCREMENT | |
| `run_id` | TEXT | FK → pipeline_runs.id, NOT NULL | |
| `round_number` | INTEGER | NOT NULL | 1-based |
| `drafter_role` | TEXT | NOT NULL | `hermes-v4pro` |
| `drafter_output` | TEXT | NOT NULL | Full Drafter response |
| `reviewer_role` | TEXT | NOT NULL | `hermes-r1` |
| `reviewer_signal` | TEXT | NOT NULL | `OBJECTIONS`, `CONSENSUS_REACHED`, or `ESCALATE` |
| `objections_json` | TEXT | | JSON array of objection strings, NULL if consensus |
| `revision_number` | INTEGER | DEFAULT 1 | Increments on Drafter rework of same proposal |

## Smoke Test Objection Classification

### Objection 1: Research/Evidence gateway missing from pipeline

**Summary:** The state machine (both current orchestrator and proposed 7-stage model) omits the Research/Evidence gateway (Flash on port 8642 via NeMo 8800). No GATHER_EVIDENCE stage exists before or alongside DRAFT. The Reviewer can flag missing evidence but there's no mechanism to invoke Research.

**Blocks Tier 4 SQLite?** **No.** The spine schema can include a `research_artifacts` table regardless of whether the orchestrator calls Research.

**Classification:** **Tier 6 integration requirement.** The orchestrator needs a GATHER_EVIDENCE stage before DRAFT, re-triggerable by Reviewer at REVIEW stage. This requires orchestrator.py to call the Research gateway via `/api/advisor/chat?agent=hermes-prime`.

### Objection 2: Role boundary violation in EXECUTE→DRAFT failure path

**Summary:** The proposed state machine assigns "Reviewer annotation" to the EXECUTE→DRAFT rework path. Reviewer role boundary (from memory) is: "challenge proposals and identify missing evidence ONLY — never execute, never claim Worker findings as own." Annotating an implementation failure is execution-adjacent and violates this boundary.

**Blocks Tier 4 SQLite?** **No.**

**Classification:** **Tier 6 integration requirement.** Replace "Reviewer annotation" with "Implementer self-annotation" on failure. Implementer records what failed; Reviewer only challenges the revised proposal. Schema needs a `failure_annotation` column with a `source_role` discriminator.

### Objection 3: CONVERGE deadlock breaker not testable

**Summary:** The proposed CONVERGE stage uses "max 3 cycles" as a deadlock breaker but doesn't define what resets the counter. "3 cycles total" vs. "3 cycles per stage" vs. "3 consecutive Drafter revisions with no progress" — ambiguous. Without a testable definition, the orchestrator can stall indefinitely.

**Blocks Tier 4 SQLite?** **No.**

**Classification:** **Tier 6 integration requirement.** The orchestrator config needs a `deadlock_breaker` field: `max_consecutive_revisions: 3` with a `revision_counter` that resets when Reviewer emission changes from OBJECTIONS to a new signal type (e.g., CLARIFICATION_REQUESTED).

---

### Summary

| # | Objection | Blocks Tier 4? | Classification |
|---|-----------|:---:|----------------|
| 1 | Research/Evidence gateway missing | No | Tier 6 integration |
| 2 | Role boundary violation (Reviewer annotating failures) | No ...[truncated]

**Classification:** **Tier 6 integration requirement.** Replace "Reviewer annotation" with "Implementer self-annotation" on failure. Implementer records what failed; Reviewer only challenges the revised proposal. Schema needs a `failure_annotation` column with a `source_role` discriminator.

**Summary:** The proposed CONVERGE stage uses "max 3 cycles" as a deadlock breaker but doesn't define what resets the counter. **Blocks Tier 4 SQLite?** **No.**

**Classification:** **Tier 6 integration requirement.** The orchestrator config needs a `deadlock_breaker` field: `max_consecutive_revisions: 3` with a `revision_counter` that resets when Reviewer emission changes from OBJECTIONS to a new signal type (e.g., CLARIFICATION_REQUESTED).

## Smoke Test Objection Classification

### Objection 1: Research/Evidence gateway missing from pipeline

**Summary:** The state machine (both current orchestrator and proposed 7-stage model) omits the Research/Evidence gateway (Flash on port 8642 via NeMo 8800). No GATHER_EVIDENCE stage exists before or alongside DRAFT. The Reviewer can flag missing evidence but there's no mechanism to invoke Research.

**Blocks Tier 4 SQLite?** **No.** The spine schema can include a `research_artifacts` table regardless of whether the orchestrator calls Research.

**Classification:** **Tier 6 integration requirement.** The orchestrator needs a GATHER_EVIDENCE stage before DRAFT, re-triggerable by Reviewer at REVIEW stage. This requires orchestrator.py to call the Research gateway via `/api/advisor/chat?agent=hermes-prime`.

### Objection 2: Role boundary violation in EXECUTE→DRAFT failure path

**Summary:** The proposed state machine assigns "Reviewer annotation" to the EXECUTE→DRAFT rework path. Reviewer role boundary (from memory) is: "challenge proposals and identify missing evidence ONLY — never execute, never claim Worker findings as own." Annotating an implementation failure is execution-adjacent and violates this boundary.

**Blocks Tier 4 SQLite?** **No.**

**Classification:** **Tier 6 integration requirement.** Replace "Reviewer annotation" with "Implementer self-annotation" on failure. Implementer records what failed; Reviewer only challenges the revised proposal. Schema needs a `failure_annotation` column with a `source_role` discriminator.

### Objection 3: CONVERGE deadlock breaker not testable

**Summary:** The proposed CONVERGE stage uses "max 3 cycles" as a deadlock breaker but doesn't define what resets the counter. "3 cycles total" vs. "3 cycles per stage" vs. "3 consecutive Drafter revisions with no progress" — ambiguous. Without a testable definition, the orchestrator can stall indefinitely.

**Blocks Tier 4 SQLite?** **No.**

**Classification:** **Tier 6 integration requirement.** The orchestrator config needs a `deadlock_breaker` field: `max_consecutive_revisions: 3` with a `revision_counter` that resets when Reviewer emission changes from OBJECTIONS to a new signal type (e.g., CLARIFICATION_REQUESTED).

---

| 1 | Research/Evidence gateway missing | No | Tier 6 integration |
| 2 | Role boundary violation (Reviewer annotating failures) | No ...[truncated]

### Table 1: `pipeline_runs` (Tier 4.1 — REQUIRED)

**Purpose:** One row per orchestrator deliberation session.

| Column | Type | Constraint | Description |

| `topic` | TEXT | NOT NULL | The deliberation topic |
| `result` | TEXT | NOT NULL | `CONSENSUS_REACHED` or `ESCALATE` |
| `requires_eric_review` | INTEGER | DEFAULT 1 | 1 if Eric must approve (always true for now) |
| `max_rounds` | INTEGER | NOT NULL | Configured max before escalation |
| `rounds_completed` | INTEGER | NOT NULL | Actual rounds that ran |
| `created_at` | TEXT | NOT NULL | ISO8601 |
| `completed_at` | TEXT | | ISO8601, NULL if still running |

### Table 2: `deliberation_rounds` (Tier 4.1 — REQUIRED)

**Purpose:** One row per DRAFT→REVIEW round. Tracks revision counter for deadlock detection (Objection 3). Captures Reviewer signal and objections.

|--------|------|------------|-------------|
| `id` | INTEGER | PK AUTOINCREMENT | |
| `run_id` | TEXT | FK → pipeline_runs.id, NOT NULL | |
| `round_number` | INTEGER | NOT NULL | 1-based |
| `drafter_role` | TEXT | NOT NULL | `hermes-v4pro` |
| `drafter_output` | TEXT | NOT NULL | Full Drafter response |
| `reviewer_role` | TEXT | NOT NULL | `hermes-r1` |
| `reviewer_signal` | TEXT | NOT NULL | `OBJECTIONS`, `CONSENSUS_REACHED`, or `ESCALATE` |
| `objections_json` | TEXT | | JSON array of objection strings, NULL if consensus |
| `revision_number` | INTEGER | DEFAULT 1 | Increments on Drafter rework of same proposal |
| `requires_eric_review` | INTEGER | DEFAULT 1 | From structured Reviewer signal |
| `created_at` | TEXT | NOT NULL | ISO8601 |

**Deadlock tracking (Objection 3):** `revision_number` tracks consecutive Drafter revisions. A `deadlock_detected` condition is: `revision_number >= max_consecutive_revisions AND reviewer_signal = 'OBJECTIONS'`. Configurable in orchestrator, verifiable in SQL.

### Table 3: `research_artifacts` (DEFERRED — Tier 4.2+)

**Purpose:** Evidence gathered by Research/Evidence gateway. Addresses Objection 1 (GATHER_EVIDENCE stage absent from pipeline).

| Column | Type | Constraint | Description |
|--------|------|---------- ...[truncated]

That's a router rule, not a toolset restriction. And the router already exists in v0.1 with classify and dispatch. The blocker is that the router currently classifies by model capability, not by CIS role permission — it would happily route an implementation request to any gateway that can answer it.

But the orchestrator state machine in Tier 0 doesn't touch the router. And the router reclassification is Tier 7.

So the gap is real but the fix location is different than I initially said: not terminal toolset config, but gateway routing rules that enforce the Drafter/Reviewer/Implementer role boundary at the API dispatch layer.
```

I receive an API call, I generate a response, I return it. I can't call `write_file` or `terminal` because the browser interface doesn't expose those tools — those are CLI-only.

That's a router rule, not a toolset restriction. And the router already exists in v0.1 with classify and dispatch. The blocker is that the router currently classifies by model capability, not by CIS role permission — it would happily route an implementation request to any gateway that can answer it.

But the orchestrator state machine in Tier 0 doesn't touch the router. And the router reclassification is Tier 7.

So the gap is real but the fix location is different than I initially said: not terminal toolset config, but gateway routing rules that enforce the Drafter/Reviewer/Implementer role boundary at the API dispatch layer.
```

# CIS current-context briefing — loaded when HERMES_CIS_BRIEFING_PATH
# points at a valid file.  Independent of skip_context_files so it
# loads even when project-level AGENTS.md / .cursorrules are skipped.

For CLI mode (terminal sessions like this one), a new AIAgent is created per session, so the briefing is read at session start.

evidence_rule: |
  CIS must not rely on trust-based agent self-reporting.
  Every consequential agent response must be accompanied by one of:
    1. Raw local evidence:
       - command and raw terminal output
       - git status/show output
       - file contents or grep output
       - database query output
       - test output

       - retrieved document reference

  "no mutation," "ready to commit," or "complete" are incomplete

       - database query output

ok now take into account claudes recommendations. 
ChatGPT's diagnosis is correct and the proposed fix is the right direction. Let me go deeper on what this actually exposes and what the full implications are.

The core design flaw: deterministic process, non-deterministic inputs
The system was built around a principle of deterministic verification — gate scripts that exit 0 or non-zero, no self-reporting, evidence-based completion. That discipline was applied to outputs. It was never applied to generator inputs.
The result is a false sense of rigor. gate_export_agreement.sh can verify that AGENTS.md matches the manifest hash. It cannot verify that the manifest hash corresponds to a semantically current state. You have a hash-verified lie. The pipeline produces consistent, reproducible output that is consistently, reproducibly wrong about where the project stands.
This is worse than having no gate at all, because the gate creates confidence that isn't warranted.

Why this happened: the bootstrapping trap
The export pipeline was built to solve manual drift. While it was being built, the state it was supposed to encode had to come from somewhere — so hardcoded strings were used as a temporary measure. That's a reasonable scaffolding choice. The mistake was that no explicit gate or convention marked those strings as temporary, and no ticket or blocker was created saying "these strings must be replaced before the export pipeline is considered complete."
Tier 5 was declared complete when the mechanical pipeline worked. The semantic correctness of the pipeline's inputs was never a stated exit criterion for Tier 5. So the scaffolding became permanent by default.
This is the bootstrapping trap: you can't derive build state from the spine before the spine exists, so you hardcode it. But once the spine exists, you have to go back and remove the hardcoding. That second step requires an explicit gate. Without it, the scaffolding persists indefinitely.

Hidden instances of the same problem
This almost certainly isn't isolated to two files. Anywhere a human wrote a string describing project state into a config file or generator — rather than querying the spine — is a candidate for the same issue. The audit in step 1 of ChatGPT's directive needs to be genuinely exhaustive, not just the four files listed. Specifically:

Any README or CHANGELOG generated by the export pipeline that has hardcoded tier language
Any session orientation templates that reference a current phase ...[truncated]

ChatGPT's diagnosis is correct and the proposed fix is the right direction. Let me go deeper on what this actually exposes and what the full implications are.

The core design flaw: deterministic process, non-deterministic inputs
The system was built around a principle of deterministic verification — gate scripts that exit 0 or non-zero, no self-reporting, evidence-based completion. That discipline was applied to outputs. It was never applied to generator inputs.
The result is a false sense of rigor. gate_export_agreement.sh can verify that AGENTS.md matches the manifest hash. It cannot verify that the manifest hash corresponds to a semantically current state. You have a hash-verified lie. The pipeline produces consistent, reproducible output that is consistently, reproducibly wrong about where the project stands.
This is worse than having no gate at all, because the gate creates confidence that isn't warranted.

Why this happened: the bootstrapping trap
The export pipeline was built to solve manual drift. While it was being built, the state it was supposed to encode had to come from somewhere — so hardcoded strings were used as a temporary measure. That's a reasonable scaffolding choice. The mistake was that no explicit gate or convention marked those strings as temporary, and no ticket or blocker was created saying "these strings must be replaced before the export pipeline is considered complete."
Tier 5 was declared complete when the mechanical pipeline worked. The semantic correctness of the pipeline's inputs was never a stated exit criterion for Tier 5. So the scaffolding became permanent by default.
This is the bootstrapping trap: you can't derive build state from the spine before the spine exists, so you hardcode it. But once the spine exists, you have to go back and remove the hardcoding. That second step requires an explicit gate. Without it, the scaffolding persists indefinitely.

Hidden instances of the same problem
This almost certainly isn't isolated to two files. Anywhere a human wrote a string describing project state into a config file or generator — rather than querying the spine — is a candidate for the same issue. The audit in step 1 of ChatGPT's directive needs to be genuinely exhaustive, not just the four files listed. Specifically:

Any README or CHANGELOG generated by the export pipeline that has hardcoded tier language
Any session orientation templates that reference a current phase ...[truncated]

This is worse than having no gate at all, because the gate creates confidence that isn't warranted.

Why this happened: the bootstrapping trap
The export pipeline was built to solve manual drift. While it was being built, the state it was supposed to encode had to come from somewhere — so hardcoded strings were used as a temporary measure. That's a reasonable scaffolding choice. The mistake was that no explicit gate or convention marked those strings as temporary, and no ticket or blocker was created saying "these strings must be replaced before the export pipeline is considered complete."
Tier 5 was declared complete when the mechanical pipeline worked. The semantic correctness of the pipeline's inputs was never a stated exit criterion for Tier 5. So the scaffolding became permanent by default.
This is the bootstrapping trap: you can't derive build state from the spine before the spine exists, so you hardcode it. But once the spine exists, you have to go back and remove the hardcoding. That second step requires an explicit gate. Without it, the scaffolding persists indefinitely.

Hidden instances of the same problem
This almost certainly isn't isolated to two files. Anywhere a human wrote a string describing project state into a config file or generator — rather than querying the spine — is a candidate for the same issue. The audit in step 1 of ChatGPT's directive needs to be genuinely exhaustive, not just the four files listed. Specifically:

Any README or CHANGELOG generated by the export pipeline that has hardcoded tier language
Any session orientation templates that reference a current phase ...[truncated]
